scenes.tts: Why can oysters live in the lower James River but not near Richmond? Follow one Virginia landscape from mountain forest to salty Bay, and look for both kinds of clues. Some clues are alive. Others are parts of the surroundings.
scenes.visual: Hook first, no title. Fill the frame with one continuous Virginia cross-section: mountain forest at left, rocky stream becoming the James, wide Chesapeake Bay, then ocean at right. A small boat drifts downstream. An oyster reef grows in the lower river while a ghosted oyster near Richmond fades out. Camera glides along the river with moving water. COLOR MAP FOR BOTH FILMS: living things GREEN, nonliving conditions GOLD, fresh water BLUE, mixed estuary water TEAL, salt water PURPLE, oysters RED, labels TEXT white. At most six labeled objects.
scenes.narration: Why can oysters live in the lower James River but not near Richmond? Follow one Virginia landscape from mountain forest to salty Bay, and look for both kinds of clues. Some clues are alive. Others are parts of the surroundings.

scenes.visual: Keep the moving cross-section dimly visible. Show the title 'Two Sides of Every Ecosystem' for two seconds, then transform the title into two large outlined lenses over the same landscape.

scenes.tts: An ecosystem includes all living things in a place and their nonliving surroundings. The living side includes plants, animals, fungi, microorganisms, and their interactions. Watch a deer eat acorns while fungi spread through a fallen log. These relationships are biotic factors.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the forest without changing worlds. A GREEN outline grows around the deer, oak, fungi, and tiny microorganism dots. Animate the deer lowering its head to acorns and fungal threads spreading through one log. The left lens fills GREEN and gains the short label 'biotic: living'.
scenes.narration: An ecosystem includes all living things in a place and their nonliving surroundings. The living side includes plants, animals, fungi, microorganisms, and their interactions. Watch a deer eat acorns while fungi spread through a fallen log. These relationships are biotic factors.

scenes.tts: The nonliving side includes climate, sunlight, water, soil, air, and nutrients. These are abiotic factors. Rain darkens the soil while sunlight shifts under the tree canopy. Both sides share one place, and changes on either side can matter.
scenes.visual: Carry the same forest. GOLD sunbeams sweep across leaves, BLUE rain falls, a breeze bends grass, and soil darkens. The right lens fills GOLD and gains 'abiotic: nonliving'. Slide both lenses together until they overlap over the forest; keep deer and rain moving.
scenes.narration: The nonliving side includes climate, sunlight, water, soil, air, and nutrients. These are abiotic factors. Rain darkens the soil while sunlight shifts under the tree canopy. Both sides share one place, and changes on either side can matter.

scenes.tts: Now the forest canopy grows thicker, but everything else stays the same. Less sunlight reaches the forest floor. What do you predict will happen to the small plants below?
scenes.visual: Branches and leaves slowly close across the upper half of the same forest. GOLD sunbeams narrow, but three GREEN floor plants remain visible. Put the question 'What happens below?' large at center. Do not reveal an answer. Leaves keep swaying.
scenes.narration: Now the forest canopy grows thicker, but everything else stays the same. Less sunlight reaches the forest floor. What do you predict will happen to the small plants below?

scenes.visual: Hold the prediction question for four and a half seconds. Keep leaves swaying and the narrow sunbeams shimmering. The floor plants remain unchanged during the thinking pause.

scenes.tts: The shaded plants grow poorly or disappear from the picture. Light is one condition that can limit where plants survive. Deep or muddy water can block light too. That helps explain why few plants grow on some underwater floors.
scenes.visual: Reveal two floor plants shrinking and fading while the plant in a small light patch remains. Transform the forest floor into a cutaway of deep, muddy estuary water in the same lower frame. Suspended GOLD-brown mud blocks descending light; plants vanish below the dim zone. Mark the cutaway 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: The shaded plants grow poorly or disappear from the picture. Light is one condition that can limit where plants survive. Deep or muddy water can block light too. That helps explain why few plants grow on some underwater floors.

scenes.tts: Climate is the usual pattern of temperature and rainfall over many years. Earth's tilt changes sunlight angle and day length as Earth travels around the sun. Latitude, elevation, land shape, and human actions also shape climate. Climate is part of the abiotic side.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the Virginia cross-section. Above it, show a simple tilted Earth moving along a short curved orbit segment while sunbeams change angle; label the orbit 'schematic'. Below, cycle the same landscape through rain, summer sun, and winter snow. Raise the mountain and lower the coast while a GOLD climate ribbon spans the scene.
scenes.narration: Climate is the usual pattern of temperature and rainfall over many years. Earth's tilt changes sunlight angle and day length as Earth travels around the sun. Latitude, elevation, land shape, and human actions also shape climate. Climate is part of the abiotic side.

scenes.tts: Carry the same paired view across Virginia. A forest is a terrestrial ecosystem on land. A mountain stream is freshwater, with very little salt. Ocean water is marine and salty. Between them, an estuary mixes fresh river water with salty ocean water.
scenes.visual: Pan left to right across the carried cross-section. Place four large labels in sequence: 'terrestrial', 'freshwater', 'estuary', 'marine'. BLUE stream water flows into TEAL mixed water as PURPLE ocean water pulses inland with a tide. Tiny salt dots increase toward the ocean.
scenes.narration: Carry the same paired view across Virginia. A forest is a terrestrial ecosystem on land. A mountain stream is freshwater, with very little salt. Ocean water is marine and salty. Between them, an estuary mixes fresh river water with salty ocean water.

scenes.tts: These labels describe surroundings, not empty containers. Organisms must handle those conditions while also finding food and meeting other living things. Living interactions and nonliving conditions help decide what can live where. That rule may explain the oyster puzzle, but we need evidence along the river.
scenes.visual: Remove the setting labels and let GREEN organism icons test the carried landscape: a tree settles on land, a stream insect settles in BLUE water, and an oyster tests the TEAL lower river. GOLD condition arrows and GREEN interaction arrows converge on each icon. The oyster near Richmond fades while the lower-river oyster remains.
scenes.narration: These labels describe surroundings, not empty containers. Organisms must handle those conditions while also finding food and meeting other living things. Living interactions and nonliving conditions help decide what can live where. That rule may explain the oyster puzzle, but we need evidence along the river.

scenes.tts: No single factor tells the whole story. A suitable condition does not prove an organism was present. A range match is a clue, not a complete answer. Ecosystems also change as conditions, populations, and species change. The next step is to test one condition along the James.
scenes.visual: Keep the James cross-section full frame. Add a clear check mark labeled 'could fit' beside the lower-river oyster, then keep a separate empty observation box labeled 'counted here?' with no check. Water continues moving and the salinity-color boundary gently shifts. Fade all labels before the end card.
scenes.narration: No single factor tells the whole story. A suitable condition does not prove an organism was present. A range match is a clue, not a complete answer. Ecosystems also change as conditions, populations, and species change. The next step is to test one condition along the James.

scenes.visual: End card shows one line only, centered at high contrast: 'Living interactions and nonliving conditions help decide what can live where.' No title, subtitle, logo, or smaller line.
